paper_context.research_question: Can a unified macro-micro discourse representation that incorporates primary-secondary (nuclearity) relations at both micro (rhetorical/semantic) and macro (schematic/pragmatic) levels be defined and used to build a corpus (MCDTB) for analyzing and recognizing discourse relations and primary-secondary relations in Chinese newswire?
main_claims: A macro-micro unified discourse representation schema that combines micro-level rhetorical (logical/semantic) relations and macro-level schematic (pragmatic/function) relations, with an explicit primary-secondary relation, is appropriate for discourse structure analysis.
The authors constructed a Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB) of 97 Xinhua newswire articles annotated with macro schematic roles, micro rhetorical relations, and primary-secondary labels.

Preliminary classification experiments (10-fold cross-validation, maxent classifiers with listed features) show the corpus enables reasonable performance on primary-secondary relation recognition (e.g., reported F-scores: P-S 79.3%, S-P 88.9%, MP 50.0%) and moderate performance on discourse relation recognition (e.g., several relations with F-scores 28.6%–66.7%), supporting the resource's utility.

Annotation strategy (top-down + bottom-up), quality-assurance measures (agreement/Kappa on a 20-document subset), and the chosen tree representation are feasible for capturing macro discourse structure in news genre.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Corpus coverage and representativeness (size, genre selection, paragraph/sentence statistics)
Annotation schema clarity and expressiveness (definition of node types, relation categories, primary-secondary types)
Annotation quality and inter-annotator agreement (reported agreement/Kappa on subset, consistency across layers)
Task baseline performance (primary-secondary recognition and discourse relation classification metrics, class imbalance handling)
Reproducibility and tooling (annotation procedure, guidelines, feature set, classifier settings)
Novelty relative to prior discourse resources (integration of macro schematic roles with micro rhetorical structure in Chinese)
Scalability and generalizability (whether schema and annotation strategy extend beyond newswire and to larger corpora)

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If annotators still disagree despite full-article context, inter-annotator agreement will be low and labels may be unreliable for learning or analysis.

argument_focus: Definition and formalization of a macro-micro unified discourse representation that includes primary-secondary relations at both levels.
Construction details and statistics of the Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB).
Annotation protocol (top-down + bottom-up), QA procedure (agreement/Kappa on subset), and representational choices (paragraph-as-leaves, relation taxonomy).
Preliminary classification baselines and performance for primary-secondary and discourse relation recognition, including feature sets and resampling choices.
contribution_targets: A resource: MCDTB — 97 annotated Chinese newswire articles with macro schematic roles, micro rhetorical relations, and primary-secondary labels.
A representation/schema: Macro-micro unified discourse tree combining schematic (macro) and rhetorical (micro) relations with explicit primary-secondary distinctions.
Empirical baselines: initial experiments (maxent, 10-fold CV) for primary-secondary recognition and discourse relation classification and their reported results.
evaluation_targets: Reproducibility of corpus construction: access to annotated files, annotation guidelines, and complete statistics (per-class supports, Table 4 values).
Validity and reliability of annotations: full inter-annotator agreement/Kappa values for all layers and conflict-resolution protocol.
Representational coverage: whether the relation taxonomy and schematic categories cover observed phenomena (counts and examples of out-of-vocabulary relations or ad-hoc labels).
Experimental methodology: details of resampling procedure, classifier hyperparameters, feature extraction, and per-class supports to interpret F-scores, especially for small classes.

chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should (a) request or verify the full annotation guidelines and release package (annotated files, schema documentation), (b) examine Table 4 raw agreement/Kappa numbers and layer-wise inter-annotator disagreement examples, (c) inspect per-class instance counts and exact resampling code/strategy to reproduce reported baseline experiments, and (d) evaluate whether the mapping between micro relations and macro schematic functions was formalized or left to annotator judgment (to test assumption A7).

Experimental checks to run: re-run baselines with stratified sampling and alternative classifiers (e.g., logistic regression with regularization, SVM, tree ensembles) and perform statistical significance tests for reported F-scores, especially for small classes.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues for a unified macro-micro discourse representation that explicitly encodes primary-secondary (nuclearity) relations at both micro (rhetorical) and macro (schematic) levels, instantiates that representation by annotating 97 Xinhua newswire articles to produce MCDTB, and reports baseline classification results for primary-secondary recognition and discourse relation labeling. The reasoning chain: theoretical motivation (gap in prior work treating nuclearity only at micro/rhetorical level), design of representation (paragraphs as macro leaves, taxonomy of relations, macro schematic roles inspired by Van Dijk), annotation protocol (top-down + bottom-up; local/global principles for nucleus judgment), corpus statistics and co-occurrence observations (relation ↔ nucleus distributions), and preliminary supervised experiments (resampling, maxent classifiers, reported F-scores). The argument succeeds in conceptually motivating the unified schema and demonstrating feasibility via a small resource and baseline experiments. Weak links include incomplete reporting of inter-annotator agreement values across annotation layers, underspecified resampling and experimental details, limited statistical treatment of corpus observations (no tests for dependence, unstable counts for rare classes), and potential conflation of annotation-guideline constraints with empirical patterns (e.g., all Joint labeled MP). Overall, the manuscript presents a plausible new resource and schema, but several methodological and reporting gaps limit confidence in the generality and robustness of claimed findings.

Edge B→C

Edge E→F

strengths.title: Clear conceptual motivation to integrate nuclearity at macro scale
strengths.description: The paper articulates a coherent gap: existing work often treats nuclearity at micro/rhetorical level but not as an independent, macro-level task; the unified schema addresses this conceptual gap with explicit definitions and examples.
evidence: Introduction framing importance of primary-secondary relationship and its under-exploration.
Section 3 definitions and Figures 4–7 illustrating macro-micro trees and arrows for nucleus.

strengths.title: Concrete resource creation with detailed taxonomy
strengths.description: Authors constructed a non-trivial annotated resource (97 documents) that combines macro schematic labels and micro rhetorical relations with nucleus annotations and provide per-relation counts.
evidence: Section 4.1 and 4.4: statement of corpus size and Table 5 and Table 6 counts.
Table 3: 15-subcategory relation taxonomy.

strengths.title: Provision of baseline experiments and feature list
strengths.description: The paper does not stop at resource release; it runs 10-fold CV baselines for both nucleus recognition and relation classification and lists engineered features (structural, TF-IDF word pairs, first-words+POS, similarity to title, hierarchical positions).
evidence: Section 5 and Table 7: features and experimental setup.
Tables 8 and 9: reported baseline metrics.

strengths.title: Use of established theoretical grounding
strengths.description: The schema is grounded in recognized discourse theories (RST for micro, Van Dijk for macro), which supports interpretability and ties to prior literature.
evidence: Sections 2 and 3 reference RST, Van Dijk, and CDT (Li et al. 2014).
Figures and mapping between micro relations and macro schematic functions.

concerns.title: Incomplete reporting of inter-annotator agreement across layers
concerns.description: The manuscript reports that agreement and Kappa were measured on 20 documents but provides no numeric values for the reported layers (leaf-only), leaving the reliability of higher-level annotations (relations, nucleus at non-leaf nodes, macro schematic roles) unquantified.
evidence: Section 4.3: 'Table 4 illustrates the annotation consistency in detail.' but Table 4 values are absent in the provided extract; text also states 'Our measurement data is only taken on the layer of leaf nodes.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include complete agreement/Kappa numbers for all annotation layers (leaf, non-leaf relations, nucleus labels, macro schematic functions), provide confusion matrices and qualitative examples of disagreements and their resolution.

concerns.title: Underspecified resampling and experimental details
concerns.description: Resampling is applied (nucleus-in-latter multiplied ten times) but the full resampling protocol, per-class instance counts, stratification procedure, classifier hyperparameters, and random seeds are not provided — making results hard to reproduce and possibly biased by overfitting.
evidence: Section 5: only brief note 're-sampling the data set of nucleus in latter to ten times' and 'NLTK default maxent' without per-class supports or reproducibility artifacts.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-class instance counts before/after resampling, cross-validation fold construction, classifier hyperparameters and random seeds; run additional baselines (regularized logistic regression, SVM, tree ensembles) and report statistical significance or confidence intervals.

concerns.title: Potential annotation guideline bias inflating corpus patterns
concerns.description: Tables show deterministic patterns (e.g., all Joint relations labeled MP; all Elaboration labeled P-S). It is unclear whether these patterns reflect linguistic regularities or arise from annotation guidelines that forced specific nucleus assignments for relation types.
evidence: Table 6: Joint 151→151 MP; Elaboration 121→121 P-S; Background 47→47 P-S; strong one-to-one mapping in many categories.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify whether nucleus assignment rules were constrained by relation type in guidelines. If not constrained, provide annotator decision examples and perform an analysis to show that joint→MP observations hold across independent annotators.

concerns.title: Granularity assumption of paragraphs as macro leaves not validated
concerns.description: The paper assumes paragraphs are appropriate atomic units for macro annotation (A1). No empirical test (e.g., mapping to EDUs, measuring intra-paragraph relation variance) is provided to validate that paragraph boundaries preserve necessary rhetorical distinctions.
evidence: Section 3.1: 'on the macro layer, we directly treat the paragraphs... as leaf nodes.' and examples only.
Chaining notes recommend testing paragraph-vs-EDU effects.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include a small-scale comparison where several documents are additionally annotated at EDU granularity or mapped to existing CDTB EDUs to quantify information loss or differences in nucleus decisions when using paragraphs vs. EDUs.

concerns.title: Limited corpus size and genre scope for generalization claims
concerns.description: Resource consists of 97 Xinhua newswire documents only; claims about schema appropriateness and utility lack evidence across other news sources, subgenres, or longer documents (chapters), limiting claims of generalizability.
evidence: Section 4.4: corpus drawn exclusively from Chinese Treebank 8.0 Xinhua articles; Conclusion notes future enlargement as future work.
No cross-genre tests provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Temper claims about generalizability in text; if possible, add a small held-out set from a different news source or genre to test portability, or explicitly state scope limitations.

concerns.title: Insufficient statistical analysis of corpus observations
concerns.description: The observed dependence between relation types and nucleus distributions is asserted but not formally tested (no chi-square, Fisher's exact, or effect-size measures), and many relation categories have low counts, raising stability concerns.
evidence: Section 4.4: 'The statistics shows the relationship between discourse relation and primary-secondary relation is strong dependence' but no formal statistical evidence provided; Table 6 shows low counts for several categories.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct and report formal statistical tests for dependence (with caveats for small counts), and aggregate rare relation classes where appropriate to increase stability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a unified macro-micro discourse representation that (a) treats paragraphs as macro-level leaf nodes, (b) combines micro rhetorical relations (RST/CDT-like) with macro schematic functions (Van Dijk-inspired), and (c) annotates explicit primary-secondary (nuclearity) at both micro and macro layers. The authors built MCDTB: 97 Xinhua newswire articles (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations) annotated with micro relations (15 subcategories), macro schematic roles, and primary-secondary labels (P-S, S-P, MP). They report inter-annotator consistency measured on a 20-document subset (leaf-layer only) and present baseline classifiers (NLTK maxent, feature set listed, 10-fold CV, resampling minority class) for primary-secondary recognition and discourse relation classification with per-class precision/recall/F-scores. The paper's central methodological claims are: the schema is expressive and feasible for newswire, the corpus is a useful resource, and preliminary experiments demonstrate learnability of labels. For these claims to hold, several methodological and reproducibility conditions must be true: (1) annotation guidelines and conflict-resolution protocols must yield reliable labels across layers (not just leaves); (2) the choice of paragraph-as-leaf must not systematically hide intra-paragraph rhetorical phenomena critical to nuclearity; (3) reported experimental settings (resampling, per-class supports, hyperparameters) must be fully specified and available so performance is interpretable and reproducible. Evidence provided supports feasibility on a small, in-genre sample, but is insufficient to establish generalizability, statistical stability for small classes, and the absence of annotation-induced dependencies between relation types and nucleus labels. I list concrete weaknesses that should be addressed (missing release of artifacts, incomplete agreement metrics, incomplete resampling details, potential annotation bias where relation class implies nucleus) and provide targeted suggestions to strengthen reproducibility and validity.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Discourse understanding benefits from explicit nuclearity (primary-secondary) distinctions (claimed importance and prior work cited).

L2: Micro-level RST/CDT captures local rhetorical relations and nuclearity in relation-specific way; macro-level Van Dijk captures schematic/pragmatic functions — these two perspectives are complementary.

L3: A unified macro-micro representation (tree with paragraph leaves, non-leaf rhetorical relations, and schematic functions added) can represent both logical and pragmatic roles and their nuclearity simultaneously.
L4: Using this schema, a corpus (MCDTB) of 97 Xinhua articles can be annotated with macro schematic roles, micro relations, and primary-secondary labels.
L5: Inter-annotator agreement on a leaf-node subset is acceptable (Table 4 referenced), providing some evidence of annotation reliability.

L6: Baseline classifiers (maxent, listed features, 10-fold CV, resampling minority) achieve reasonable per-class performance for primary-secondary recognition and moderate performance for several relation classes, indicating labels are learnable.
L7: Therefore, the schema and corpus are appropriate and useful for discourse structure analysis in the news genre.

Critical dependencies (edges): L3 depends on L2; L4 depends on L3 and feasibility of annotation strategy; L5 must hold across layers for L4 to support reliability claims; L6 depends on faithful resampling and sufficient per-class instances; L7 requires L5 and L6 to generalize beyond the annotated subset.

concerns.description: The schema assumes paragraphs are appropriate atomic units for macro analysis. No empirical check (e.g., mapping from EDUs to paragraphs, analysis of intra-paragraph heterogeneous relations) is provided to show this granularity preserves critical rhetorical/nuclear signals.

Alternatively, justify paragraph granularity with quantitative evidence (e.g., >X% paragraphs internally coherent).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a unified macro-micro discourse representation that explicitly encodes primary-secondary (nuclearity) relations at both macro (schematic/pragmatic) and micro (rhetorical/semantic) levels, operationalizes this schema for news articles, and releases a small Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB, 97 Xinhua documents) annotated with macro schematic roles, micro rhetorical relations, and primary-secondary labels. The authors argue that paragraph-level leaves, a taxonomy of 15 micro relations, and top-down + bottom-up annotation yield a feasible annotation workflow; they validate feasibility via inter-annotator checks on a 20-document subset and run baseline classification experiments (maxent, 10-fold CV, resampling) for nucleus recognition and relation classification. The paper's core novelty is the explicit integration of macro schematic function labels with micro rhetorical relations and a focus on nuclearity as an independent prediction target; empirical results are preliminary but suggest predictable patterns (e.g., relation-to-nucleus co-occurrence) and reasonable baseline performance for the major classes.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Nuclearity (primary-secondary) is important but often treated only within micro-level rhetorical analyses.
Observation: Discourse has both micro (RST-like) and macro (Van Dijk-style schematic) hierarchical structure; these perspectives are complementary.
Proposal: Define a macro-micro unified tree representation that places paragraphs as leaves for macro layer, retains micro-level EDUs/relations, and annotates primary-secondary at both levels.
Operationalization: Adopt a taxonomy of 15 micro relations, Van Dijk-inspired macro schematic functions, and three nucleus classes (P-S, S-P, MP); use top-down + bottom-up annotation.
Resource construction: Annotate 97 Xinhua news articles (MCDTB), produce statistics showing relation distributions and strong co-occurrence patterns between relation type and nucleus label.
Validation: Measure annotator agreement on a 20-document subset (leaf layer), then run baseline classifiers (maxent) with resampling and features to predict nucleus and relation labels.
Conclusion: Observed baseline performance and corpus statistics indicate the schema and resource are feasible for macro discourse analysis and nucleus recognition, meriting further expansion.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a macro-micro unified discourse representation that explicitly encodes 'primary-secondary' (nuclearity) relations at both micro (rhetorical) and macro (schematic/pragmatic) layers, operationalizes paragraph-as-leaf nodes at the macro level, and instantiates this schema by annotating a 97-document Chinese newswire corpus (MCDTB). The authors: (1) motivate nuclearity as an independent, essential task for discourse-aware NLP; (2) define a multi-layer tree representation combining Van Dijk-style schematic roles for news with micro rhetorical relations (15 subcategories) and three nucleus types (P-S, S-P, MP); (3) annotate 97 Xinhua articles, report corpus statistics (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations), and measure annotator consistency on a 20-document leaf-node subset; (4) present preliminary classification baselines (NLTK maxent, 10-fold CV, feature set includes structural, TF-IDF word-pairs, position and semantic-similarity features) for primary-secondary recognition and relation classification, with resampling to address class imbalance; (5) claim that (a) the representation is appropriate for discourse structure analysis, (b) MCDTB supports learning of nucleus labels and relations, and (c) there is a systematic dependence between relation type and nucleus assignment. The evidence is primarily the formalization, illustrative annotated examples, corpus counts, limited QA metrics (referenced but not fully shown), and the baseline F-scores. Key risks: small corpus size, incomplete reporting of QA and resampling details, potential annotation/labeling biases (e.g., many relation types deterministically mapped to nucleus types), and unclear release/reproducibility artifacts. The manuscript appears to introduce a conceptual frame (macro-micro unified nuclearity) that lacks many close precedents; this should be treated as a potentially disruptive idea but validated with more extensive documentation, clearer QA across layers, and replication over more data/genres.
logical_argument_graph: Claim: Nuclearity (primary-secondary) has been under-addressed as an independent task in discourse analysis and is important for downstream NLP (motivation).

Observation: Existing micro-level frameworks (RST, CDT) encode nuclearity relative to relations, while macro-level theories (Van Dijk) capture schematic/pragmatic functions but rarely combine nuclearity across levels.

Proposal: Define a unified macro-micro discourse tree representation where paragraphs are macro leaf nodes; non-leaf nodes encode rhetorical relations and schematic functions; arrows indicate primary units; nucleus types are P-S, S-P, MP.

Operationalization: Build MCDTB by annotating 97 Xinhua newswire articles according to the schema, record counts and per-relation nucleus distributions (Table 6), and perform QA on a 20-doc leaf-node subset.

Empirical test: Train baseline classifiers (NLTK maxent, 10-fold CV, described features) with resampling for class imbalance to predict primary-secondary and relation labels; report per-class precision/recall/F1 (Tables 8/9).

Inference: Reasonable macro-level F-scores for nucleus detection (e.g., P-S 79.3%, S-P 88.9%) and variable relation F-scores indicate the resource and representation are useful and appropriate for discourse structure analysis.
Conclusion / Future work: The unified schema and MCDTB enable exploration of macro discourse structure; expand corpus size and cross-genre evaluation to confirm generality.

identified_claims.claim_text: A macro-micro unified discourse representation schema that combines micro-level rhetorical (logical/semantic) relations and macro-level schematic (pragmatic/function) relations, with an explicit primary-secondary relation, is appropriate for discourse structure analysis.
identified_claims.section_anchor: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 3 Macro Discourse Representation Schema
evidence: Abstract: statement about unifying micro and macro discourse structures into MCDTB.
Section 3 describes a top-down tree with title/chapter/paragraph/microstructure/EDU; arrows indicate primary unit; schematic functions added to nodes.
Introduction: positions recognition of primary-secondary relationship as independent task and integrated into unified carrier.
uncertainty_flags: 'Appropriate' is supported mainly by conceptual justification and preliminary results on a small newswire corpus (97 docs); generality across genres untested.
Operational criteria for 'appropriateness' (coverage, reliability, task improvement) are not fully formalized or empirically shown beyond baselines.

identified_claims.claim_text: The authors constructed a Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB) of 97 Xinhua newswire articles annotated with macro schematic roles, micro rhetorical relations, and primary-secondary labels.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 4 Building a Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank; 4.4 Corpus Statistics; Table 5
evidence: Section 4.1: 'we annotate a Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank(MCDTB) consist of 97 Xinhua news wire articles.'
Table 5: counts (97 docs, 533 paragraphs, 1,339 sentences, 438 macro relations).
Section 3.2/Table 3: micro relation taxonomy used in annotations.

Extent of annotation fields released (guideline, XML/stand-off formats) is unspecified.

identified_claims.claim_text: A combined top-down and bottom-up annotation strategy is feasible and effective: top-down for overall levels and bottom-up to merge lower units by form/content similarity.
evidence: Section 4.2: explicit description of top-down then bottom-up combination, and authors state 'Our annotation work shows the strategy is effective.'
uncertainty_flags: No quantitative measure (time/cost/annotator agreement by step) provided; 'effective' asserted without operational metrics or examples of difficult cases.
Conflict resolution process and inter-annotator adjudication workflow for combined strategy are not described.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotation consistency (agreement and Cohen's Kappa) was measured on a 20-document subset for discourse structure, discourse relation, and primary-secondary relation as part of QA.
evidence: Section 4.3: 'we adopt the annotator consistency using agreement and kappa on 20 documents(chtb 0011-chtb 0030). Table 4 illustrates the annotation consistency in detail.'
uncertainty_flags: Table 4 is referenced but actual numeric values are not included in the provided extracts; measurement was taken 'only on the layer of leaf nodes', leaving higher-layer agreement unknown.
The 20-document subset may not be representative of corpus variability; no inter-annotator disagreement examples are provided.

identified_claims.claim_text: MCDTB contains 97 documents, 533 paragraphs, 1,339 sentences, average paragraphs/document 5.49, average paragraph length 2.51 sentences, and 438 macro discourse relations.
evidence: Table 5 lists the documented counts and averages for the corpus.
uncertainty_flags: Distributions (e.g., per-document relation counts, per-class supports) are summarized but not fully reported; small absolute counts for many relation types are a concern.
Corpus drawn solely from Xinhua newswire — representativeness across news subgenres or other genres is untested.

identified_claims.claim_text: Among 438 relations: 151 Joint (all MP), 121 Elaboration (all P-S), 47 Background (all P-S), and overall totals P-S 242, S-P 20, MP 176, indicating strong dependence between discourse relation type and primary-secondary labeling.

Text comment: 'The statistics shows the relationship between discourse relation and primary-secondary relation is strong dependence.'
uncertainty_flags: No statistical testing or effect sizes are reported to quantify dependence; some relation subcategories have very small counts making patterns unstable.
Possible that annotation rules or guideline constraints cause deterministic mappings (e.g., labeling all Joint as MP) rather than reflecting independent empirical regularities.

identified_claims.claim_text: Preliminary classification experiments (10-fold CV, NLTK maxent classifiers with listed features and resampling) yield primary-secondary F-scores: P-S 79.3%, S-P 88.9%, MP 50.0%; discourse relation F-scores for main types range 28.6%–66.7% (see Tables 8 and 9), supporting the resource's utility.
evidence: Section 5: experimental setup (resampling nucleus-in-latter x10, 10-fold CV, NLTK maxent default params).
Table 7 lists features; Tables 8/9 contain per-class P/R/F1 values as cited.
uncertainty_flags: Resampling details (exact protocol, whether stratified across folds, treatment of other minority classes) are underspecified; resampling may bias CV results if not performed inside training folds only.
Per-class supports (counts) are not shown alongside metrics; for small classes reported F-scores may be unstable and hard to interpret.
Use of a basic maxent baseline w/ default params leaves open whether results are due to dataset signal or classifier limitations.

identified_claims.claim_text: The chosen tree representation (paragraphs as leaf nodes, non-leaf discourse relations, arrows to indicate primary units) and macro schematic categories (inspired by Van Dijk) are feasible for capturing macro discourse structure in the news genre.

Section 3.4 explains adding pragmatic function labels to leaf and non-leaf nodes and claims tree depth corresponds to semantic depth.
uncertainty_flags: Feasibility is mainly shown via illustrative examples and small-corpus annotation; there is no systematic coverage test, nor error analysis revealing cases where the schema failed or required ad-hoc fixes.
Applicability beyond Xinhua newswire (e.g., longer narratives, multi-author styles) is not demonstrated.

identified_claims.claim_text: Recognition of primary-secondary relationships is important and under-studied as an independent task; treating it independently can support downstream NLP tasks such as MT, summarization, QA, IE and sentiment analysis.

Conclusion reinforces the claim and positions primary-secondary recognition as critical and under-explored.

No experiments in this paper demonstrate gains on downstream tasks using the nucleus labels; potential value is plausible but unproven here.

strengths.title: Novel conceptual integration of macro schematic roles with micro rhetorical nuclearity
strengths.description: The paper proposes a clear, articulated representation that brings nuclearity (primary-secondary) into the macro schematic layer and combines it with micro rhetorical relations into a unified tree.
evidence: Section 3 description of macro-micro unified tree; Figures 4-6 showing how macro schematic functions and micro rhetorical relations co-exist with primary-secondary arrows.
Introduction framing the independence of the primary-secondary task.

strengths.title: Creation of an annotated Chinese resource focused on macro structure
strengths.description: The MCDTB fills a gap by offering an explicitly macro-oriented annotated dataset for Chinese newswire with nucleus labels, which is scarce in the literature.
evidence: Section 4.1 states MCDTB contains 97 Xinhua newswire articles annotated for macro schematic roles, micro relations, and primary-secondary labels; Table 5 statistics confirm counts.
Table 3 lists the micro relation subcategories applied.

strengths.title: Illustrative examples that clarify representational choices
strengths.description: The paper provides concrete annotated examples from CTB (e.g., chtb 0019, chtb 0596) demonstrating how paragraphs are grouped and how arrows indicate primaries, aiding reproducibility of the idea.
evidence: Figures 5-7 and the paragraph-level discussion in Section 3.3 showing how primary-secondary is assigned in an example article.
Explanation of local/global principles in Section 4.1 guiding annotation decisions.

strengths.title: Initial baselines demonstrating learnability of nucleus labels
strengths.description: Simple supervised classifiers with explicit features yield reasonably high F-scores for two nucleus classes, showing the labels are not entirely random and can be learned to a degree.
evidence: Table 8 reports P-S F1 79.3% and S-P F1 88.9% under 10-fold CV with resampling.
Feature set in Table 7 includes structural, lexicon, semantic-similarity and hierarchical cues aligning with the macro-level aim.

concerns.title: Limited corpus size and single-genre sampling
concerns.description: The MCDTB consists of only 97 Xinhua news articles; this small, single-source sample limits statistical power, generalizability across news subgenres, and the stability of per-class performance for many relations with small counts.
evidence: Table 5: Count of documents 97, paragraphs 533, relations 438; Table 6 shows many relation subtypes with low counts (e.g., Purpose-Behavior 1).
Paper acknowledges plans to enlarge scale but currently provides only 97 docs.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Expand the corpus (target >500 articles) across multiple news outlets and subgenres; at minimum publish per-class supports and confidence intervals for metrics, and rerun experiments on larger or held-out source splits to test stability.

concerns.title: Insufficient inter-annotator agreement reporting for higher-level layers
concerns.description: Agreement/Kappa appears to have been measured 'only on the layer of leaf nodes' on a 20-document subset; there is little or no reported inter-annotator reliability for macro relations, primary-secondary at non-leaf levels, or schematic roles.
evidence: Section 4.3: states measurement is 'only taken on the layer of leaf nodes' and references Table 4 without numeric values in the extract.
Authors note judgments of relation and structure are 'very subjective.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report full inter-annotator agreement (raw agreement and Cohen's Kappa) for all annotation layers (macro relations, nucleus labels, schematic roles); provide examples of resolved disagreements and the adjudication protocol.

concerns.title: Potential label determinism and guideline-induced bias between relation type and nucleus
concerns.description: Table 6 shows deterministic patterns (e.g., all Joint labeled MP, all Elaboration labeled P-S); such patterns may reflect annotation conventions or implicit rules rather than independent empirical tendencies, which risks teaching models annotator heuristics.
evidence: Table 6: Joint 151 all MP; Elaboration 121 all P-S; Background 47 all P-S creates near-deterministic mappings for common relations.
Text: 'The statistics shows the relationship between discourse relation and primary-secondary relation is strong dependence.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide annotation guidelines clarifying whether certain relations were constrained to particular nucleus labels, include examples of counterexamples if allowed, and run an analysis showing nucleus labeling is not trivially determined by relation label (e.g., train a classifier that predicts nucleus solely from relation label and report its performance).

concerns.title: Underspecified resampling procedure and risk of inflated cross-validation performance
concerns.description: Resampling minority class instances by replicating 'nucleus in latter' ten times is described but not specified whether performed within training folds only; naive resampling across full dataset before CV can leak duplicates into test folds and overstate performance.
evidence: Section 5: 're-sampling the data set of nucleus in latter to ten times' with no detail on fold-level procedure; 10-fold CV used.
No discussion of alternative imbalance strategies (class-weighting, SMOTE) or statistical variance of results.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify and implement resampling strictly within each training fold during CV; report per-fold results and standard deviations; compare with alternative imbalance treatments (class-weighted loss, synthetic oversampling) and check for overfitting by using a held-out test set.

concerns.title: Limited experimental baselines and missing per-class supports
concerns.description: Use of default-parameter NLTK maxent classifier is a minimal baseline; absence of stronger baselines (regularized logistic regression, SVM, tree ensembles, neural models) and missing per-class instance counts undermines interpretation of performance numbers, especially for small classes.
evidence: Section 5: 'All our classifiers are trained using nltk package with default parameters ... maximum entropy classifier.'
Tables 8/9 present F-scores but per-class supports (n) are absent.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide per-class instance counts, include additional baselines (logistic regression with regularization, SVM, Random Forest, simple neural models), tune hyperparameters, and report statistical significance / confidence intervals for reported F-scores.

concerns.title: Paragraph-as-leaf assumption not empirically validated
concerns.description: Choosing paragraphs as macro leaf nodes is plausible but not defended empirically: paragraphs can contain multiple EDUs and mixed functions; treating paragraphs as atomic risks masking intra-paragraph nucleus or relation variation.

Chaining notes recommend testing mapping between EDU-level annotations and paragraph groupings.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide an empirical analysis showing how often EDU-level nuclearity conflicts with paragraph-level label (e.g., annotate a subset at EDU granularity or map CDTB EDUs to paragraph groups), and report examples illustrating when paragraph-level grouping is appropriate or problematic.

concerns.title: Reproducibility and artifact release unclear
concerns.description: The paper does not state whether the annotated corpus, annotation guidelines, and experimental code (resampling, feature extraction, classifier configs) will be publicly released, which limits community validation and follow-up.
evidence: No explicit mention of corpus release, code repository, or file formats in the provided extracts.
Shorthand references to CTB 8.0 for source documents exist but not to the resulting MCDTB package.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include an explicit release plan and links (or an anonymized artifact), provide annotation guidelines and sample annotated files, and release code/scripts used for preprocessing, resampling and model training.
